story:
The garage had been half-converted into something that might charitably be called a studio. Egg-crate foam lined three walls; the fourth was bare drywall with a pencil mark where someone had once measured for a shelf that never went up. A clip-on desk lamp threw a hard cone of white across a folding table. Outside, October had turned the sky the color of wet cardboard.

Harper sat on a plastic lawn chair with her notebook open on her knee. Three deadlines stacked like pancakes. She'd driven twenty minutes to ask one question and wanted an answer that fit in a paragraph.

Enoch stood behind the table, which held his laptop—a [[SCHOOL]] sticker on the lid catching the lamp's glow—a small USB microphone on a boom arm, and a half-empty [[SCHOOL]] mug with a coffee ring dark enough to read like tree rings. A [[SCHOOL]] lanyard hung from a hook on the wall behind him, holding a key that probably opened nothing anymore.

"My radio drama sounds like people talking in a room," Harper said. "No tension. What am I doing wrong with the sound design?"

"You're probably front-loading your effects." Enoch tapped the edge of the table with one finger, the way people do when they're thinking out loud. "Suspense works when the sound arrives a beat after the listener expects it, not on the beat. Delay the door creak by half a second and the audience fills that gap with dread."

"Half a second. That's it?"

"That's the core of it. Your ear is trained to predict rhythmic patterns, so when a sound lands slightly off from where you expect, your brain flags it as wrong. You can also drop all ambient noise right before a key moment. Silence is the loudest effect you have."

Harper uncapped her pen. "Okay, but I've got a scene where someone opens a basement door. Right now I've got the creak, a footstep, and a low drone all hitting at once. Too much?"

"Way too much." Enoch picked up his [[SCHOOL]] water bottle, took a sip, set it back down beside the mic. "Pick one sound to carry the moment and let the others trail. Creak first, then two full seconds of nothing, then the footstep. The drone should fade in so gradually the listener doesn't realize it's there until they're already uncomfortable."

"So I'm spacing them out instead of stacking them."

"Exactly. Layering works for chaos. Suspense is about sequence. Each sound should feel like a question the next sound only half-answers."

Harper wrote that down. She looked up. "That's useful. What about the quality of the sounds themselves? I've been pulling free samples online and they all sound clean, which feels wrong."

"They are wrong." Enoch leaned forward slightly, hands on the table's edge. "Real sounds are messy. Record yourself opening your actual basement door on your phone. Add room noise, let the mic clip a little. Imperfection reads as presence. A pristine creak sounds like a sound effect; a shaky one sounds like a door."

Harper closed her notebook, stood, reached for her coat. Her boot nudged a [[SCHOOL]] tote bag stuffed with cables on the floor. Outside the half-open garage door, the gray afternoon was doing its slow collapse into dusk.

story:
The community center piano room smelled of floor wax and old coffee, and the fluorescents overhead hummed at a frequency that registered only as a vague sense of being indoors. The choir had disbanded twenty minutes ago. Most of them were already in the parking lot, fumbling for car keys, but Wolfgang remained at the upright Yamaha, stacking hymnals into a neat pile beside his [[SCHOOL]] mug, which held the last of some cold tea. His [[SCHOOL]] lanyard dangled from his neck, a single brass key swinging gently against his chest — the supply closet, probably.

Vesna stood near the door with her coat half on, which meant she wasn't leaving yet.

"I wrote a song for my own voice, and a friend wants to sing it, but she's a mezzo — probably a fifth lower than me, maybe a bit more. What's the actual process? I mean, do I just shift everything down?"

Wolfgang set the hymnals down. "Essentially, yes. You pick a new key that sits comfortably in her range, then move every note down by the same interval. If your original is in F major and you want to drop it a fifth, you'd land in B-flat major. Same melody, same rhythms, just transplanted."

Vesna pulled her coat off again — a decision made. "Okay, that part I get. But what about the piano part? I wrote a simple arpeggiated accompaniment. Do I rewrite every single chord?"

"You do transpose every chord, yes, but you don't have to rewrite them from scratch. If you're using notation software, it'll do it for you in about ten seconds. If you wrote it by hand, the piano is your friend — play each chord in the new key and write down what your fingers land on."

"I did write it by hand. That's a lot of chords to recheck. Is there a shortcut, like a transposing wheel or something?"

"There are transposition charts, sure. I can sketch one for you in a minute — it maps each original chord to its equivalent in the target key. But honestly, for a three-minute song with repeating verse structure, you're probably looking at maybe eight unique chords total. That's a five-minute job once you sit down with it."

Vesna crossed her arms. "Eight chords, fine. But here's what worries me — the bridge has a big leap up to a high note, and I wrote it so it sits right at the top of my range. If I move the whole thing down a fifth, that note might land somewhere awkward for her register. Could it end up in a break or a weak spot?"

Wolfgang leaned against the piano's fallboard, which had a chip the shape of a thumbnail missing from its corner. "That's a real concern. A leap that works in one register can land in a passaggio or a thin area in another. What I'd do is play the bridge in the new key and listen. If that high note feels strained or thin, you can adjust just that one phrase — move the leap down to a different interval that keeps the same emotional shape but fits her voice better."

"So I'm allowed to fudge one spot?"

"You're not fudging, you're re-voicing. Arrangers do it constantly. The goal is the song sounding good in the new voice, not mathematical fidelity to the original. If that high note needs to become a fourth instead of a sixth, nobody's going to call the transposition police."

He reached into the [[SCHOOL]] tote bag resting against the piano bench and pulled out a spiral notebook. Sheet music poked from the bag's open top. He uncapped a pen and began sketching a quick interval chart — original key on the left, target key on the right, clean horizontal lines.

Vesna watched him draw. The fluorescents kept humming. Outside, the parking lot was empty now.

"So I'm allowed to fudge one spot?"

"You're not fudging, you're re-voicing. Arrangers do it constantly. The goal is the song sounding good in the new voice, not mathematical fidelity to the original. If that high note needs to become a fourth instead of a sixth, nobody's going to call the transposition police."

He reached into the [[SCHOOL]] tote bag resting against the piano bench and pulled out a spiral notebook. Sheet music poked from the bag's open top. He uncapped a pen and began sketching a quick interval chart — original key on the left, target key on the right, clean horizontal lines.

story:
The fluorescents hummed at that frequency that makes everyone look slightly unwell. Whiteboards lined three walls, dense with half-erased Lewis structures nobody had bothered to clean. The room smelled like dry-erase markers and old coffee.

Diego sat across from Claudia at the back table, turning a dry-erase cap over in his fingers like a worry stone.

"I need to know what to do about Marcus. I watched him copy from a solution sheet during the group session tonight. He didn't see me see it."

Claudia set down her [[SCHOOL]] mug — the one with the chipped handle she'd stopped noticing two years ago — and leaned forward. Her [[SCHOOL]] lanyard held her ID badge at sternum height, the photo three years out of date.

"Okay. First question — do you want to handle this yourself, or are you asking me what the center's official process is? Because those are two different conversations."

"I'm asking what I should do. Not what the handbook says. He's my best friend."

"Then talk to him directly. Pull him aside before the next session and tell him what you saw. Give him the chance to come clean on his own before it becomes a reporting situation."

Diego's jaw tightened. "And if he just denies it? Marcus will look you dead in the face and say the sky is green if it gets him out of something."

"Then you have a decision about whether you're willing to escalate it. But going to him first is the right move. It's harder for someone to stay in denial once another person has said the quiet part out loud."

"That's a lot of faith in confrontation. Last time I tried to be straight with him about something, he shut down for three weeks."

Claudia didn't flinch. She'd heard versions of this for four years. "That's a risk. But the alternative is you carrying this around and resenting him for it, which will probably do more damage to the friendship than a hard conversation will."

"What if I just pretend I didn't see it? Is that actually the worst option here?"

"It's not the worst. But you'll remember it. And next time he asks you to vouch for him on something, you'll feel it. That's the real cost of pretending — it compounds."

Diego set the cap down. "So talk to him, hope he's decent, and if he's not, I report it to the center."

"That's the shape of it, yes. And if you do report it, it doesn't have to be dramatic. You come to me, I document it, and it goes through the standard process. You don't have to be the one delivering consequences."

On her laptop a [[SCHOOL]] sticker sat slightly crooked over the manufacturer's logo. She turned the screen a few degrees, just habit.

"Fine. I'll talk to him tomorrow. Short and direct, no speech."

"Good. And Diego — if the conversation goes badly and you need to come back here and figure out next steps, that's what I'm here for. You don't have to white-knuckle the follow-through alone."

"I appreciate that. I really do. I just wish it wasn't one of those things you can't un-see."

Her hand found the [[SCHOOL]] water bottle by her elbow, turned it a quarter-rotation, set it back. "Yeah. That's the thing about paying attention. You notice stuff, and then you're responsible for what you noticed. It's not fair, but it's how it works."

Diego stood and hooked his backpack over one shoulder. "Okay. Tomorrow. Thanks, Claudia."

"Anytime. And if he surprises you and actually owns it, give him credit for that too. It costs something to admit a thing like that."

She watched him go. Her [[SCHOOL]] tote bag hung from the back of her chair, a paperback poking out. The clock ticked. The fluorescents hummed. She pulled the next appointment sheet toward her.

story:
The living room belonged to Carys, and the late-afternoon light came in sideways and made everything look slightly overexposed. The coffee table had been pushed against the wall. The carpet was covered in yellow and pink sticky notes, each bearing a name in Rohan's cramped handwriting. A half-empty bag of gummy worms sat near the sofa.

Rohan sat cross-legged on the floor, holding a pink note that said *Aunt Meera* and looking at it the way a surgeon looks at a tumor.

"Okay, so the core problem is Aunt Meera and Uncle Davi cannot be within shouting distance of each other, but they both insist on sitting near the kitchen because they like to 'help,' which really means they critique whoever's cooking."

Carys was on the sofa, legs tucked under her, a [[SCHOOL]] mug on the cushion beside her, half-full of cold tea. She fidgeted with the lanyard around her neck — [[SCHOOL]] issue, keys clipped to it — while she thought.

"Right, so you need distance without making either of them feel exiled. How many people total are we seating?"

"Fourteen. Two tables pushed together, so it's one long rectangle."

"One long rectangle is actually easier than a round table for this. You get natural zones. Put Meera at one end near the kitchen door and Davi at the other end, also near the kitchen. They each get their 'helping' position but they're separated by the full length of the table."

Rohan set the pink note down. Picked it up again. "But my grandmother sits at the head. She always sits at the head. If I put Meera at one end, grandma's displaced."

"Then grandma sits in the middle. She becomes the buffer. Nobody argues while grandma is watching them. That's not a seating plan, that's a deterrent."

"That's... actually fair. Okay, so grandma center, Meera one end, Davi the other. Now the problem is Meera's husband, Colin, who agrees with Davi about the house thing but won't say so out loud, so if they're on the same end they start whispering and Meera notices and it escalates."

Carys opened the [[SCHOOL]] notebook on her lap and began sketching a table diagram. "Split the couple. Colin sits on Meera's end but three or four seats down, with someone neutral between them. Your cousin Priya would be good there if she's a talker."

"Priya talks constantly. She once held my dad hostage for forty minutes about her sourdough starter."

"Perfect. She's a human firewall. Put her between Colin and anyone he might whisper to. She'll fill every silence with bread anecdotes and nobody will get a word in edgewise."

Rohan reached for a gummy worm, chewed it thoughtfully. "I'm going to write that down. Human firewall. My mother would love this."

"Your mother doesn't need to know the methodology. Just hand her the final arrangement and say it's tradition or something."

"She'll ask why Colin isn't next to Meera. She always asks that. She thinks married couples must sit together or it's a statement about the marriage."

"Tell her it's a European thing. Europeans do that. She won't argue with Europe."

"She absolutely will argue with Europe. She argued with Europe last Thanksgiving."

Carys's [[SCHOOL]] keychain caught the lamplight as she shifted. "Then tell her grandma requested it. Nobody questions grandma. You just said she's the deterrent."

"That's circular. I'm using grandma as the reason for the seating and also as the center of the seating. If this falls apart it all collapses at once."

"Everything collapses at once if it falls apart. That's not a design flaw, that's Thanksgiving. Just get Meera and Davi separated and let the rest be chaos management. You can't solve every edge case with fourteen people and one grudge."

Rohan crumpled the pink note, then smoothed it back out on the carpet. "Fine. I'll go with the European thing and if she pushes back I'll invoke grandma as backup. Give me the order left to right."

Carys tapped her pen against the notebook. "Meera, your uncle Sanjay, grandma, Priya, Colin, your dad, your mom, Davi. Adjust the middle seats to taste, but keep those anchors locked. And hide the gummy worms before guests arrive because if Meera sees those she'll comment on sugar and that's a whole other front."

Rohan looked at the gummy worms. Looked at the sticky notes. Began rearranging them.

story:
The fluorescent lights at Party Palace hummed at a frequency just below conscious notice, the kind that made you feel vaguely interrogated without knowing why. Huda stood at the balloon counter with her canvas tote bag slung over one shoulder and the expression of someone who had a number in mind and wanted to leave with it.

Behind the counter, Selwyn adjusted the pressure gauge on the nearest helium tank. A [[SCHOOL]] lanyard hung around his neck, holding his employee badge and a small keyring that caught the light when he moved. His [[SCHOOL]] water bottle sat beside the regulator, condensation beading on its side.

"Hi, I'm throwing a small birthday thing — maybe twelve people, a living room. How many balloons do I actually need?"

Selwyn considered this the way a structural engineer considers a load-bearing wall. "For a living room that size, you're looking at maybe twenty to twenty-five if you want it to feel festive without overwhelming the space. Are you doing a cluster arrangement or spreading them around?"

"Spreading them around, probably. Just enough that it doesn't look like a regular Tuesday."

"Then twenty is your number. You'd do a bunch of five or six near the door so people walk into something, then singles or pairs taped at different heights around the room. Varying the height is what makes it look intentional rather than sad."

Huda nodded once. "Okay, twenty. And do I need to get them all filled here, or can I do some myself?"

"You can do a mix. We'll fill the big cluster for you — that's the one that benefits from a proper helium mix so it stays up. The singles you can do with air and tape them to the wall. Saves you money and they last longer since they're not losing helium through the latex."

"So the wall ones don't even need helium?"

"Nope. Air-filled balloons taped up with a dot of mounting putty will stay put for days. Helium's really only worth it for the ones you want floating free."

Huda felt her shoulders drop a fraction. "That's actually helpful. I was worried I'd need to buy a tank."

"You definitely don't need to buy a tank for twelve people. Come in the morning of or the night before and we'll fill the helium ones. They'll hold for about twelve to fourteen hours, so timing matters more than you'd think."

"Night before might be cutting it close, then."

"Yeah, if the party's at noon, fill them that morning. If it's evening, afternoon is fine. The balloons don't deflate all at once — they get droopy and a little sad-looking around hour twelve, but they're still recognizable as balloons for a while after."

Selwyn reached under the counter for his tablet, nudging aside a [[SCHOOL]] tote bag that held his lunch. The [[SCHOOL]] keychain on his lanyard swung gently as he leaned forward. A [[SCHOOL]] laptop sticker marked the tablet's corner.

"Great. I'll take twenty, you fill the cluster of six, and I'll do the rest with air at home."

"That's a solid plan. I'd grab a few extra in case one pops during transport — maybe twenty-four total, same price tier. And pick two or three colors max. More than that starts looking like a clearance bin exploded."

"Three colors, sure. Thanks."

"No problem. Bring the balloons back if you need a refill within the week — we do that for free."

Huda pulled out her phone to note the number. Above them, the sample bunches in primary colors shifted faintly in the air conditioning, as if agreeing.
